Add isolated regression coverage and deploy the updated Jev proxy.

item.title: Record per-unit feature cutoff and Rust proof handoffs
item.body:
Reconcile #9737 with the ready state-machine, census and fresh-owner replay submissions, and keep process/staleness/measurement work explicitly open. Record the accepted #10381 feature-projection contract: existing discovery produces independent per-unit outputs with early cutoff, using the existing UnitInputs read mechanism and current-revision membership authority.

Preserve the owner-selected fixed Cargo build from #6846. Resolver/default-members build selection is not a new defect or an extension of #10381. The plan also rejects a retained workspace-wide feature product under the existing incremental-analysis rule.

Documentation only. Native coordination accepted these contract refinements; pack-authoring drift passes. Follows #11340 at exact submitted head `[redacted]`, with latest master merged. No Rust checks were run for this documentation change. Related to #9737 and #10381.

item.title: Resume the Go legacy retirement plan from the current hierarchy trial
item.body:
The remaining Go hierarchy and member-family providers still use the legacy workspace index. Resume #7509 from the landed native trial and the successor session handoff, with a current service-path baseline and an executable path through correctness, cost acceptance, the provider switch and deletion.

The service baseline reproduces 392 missing legacy targets at 110 of 1,955 calls, with no native extras or false Complete answers and byte-identical observation controls. A reviewed scratch-only experiment removes duplicate preliminary proofs; its pilot preserves candidate discovery but recovers no target, exposing delayed projection after the family allowance stops. The full intervention and direct-subtype controls are running separately. Bare TestProject results are excluded from acceptance because explicit live-store inspection confirms the profile discrepancy tracked in #11198.

Coordinator 5992a212 reviewed Milestone 1 and the precise scratch-intervention plan before implementation. All diagnostic code stays on the never-merge branch `10588-go-signature-diagnosis-scratch`. Product fixes need review of measured results and their design; the existing owner hold on the production switch remains. This PR changes only the active plan.

Validation: source wiring, historical handoff and current constructor profiles checked; frozen public-answer controls recorded on #10588 and #11198. Diff checks and pack-authoring drift pass. No Rust test applies to the plan text.

Refs #7509, #10588, #9224, #11198.

item.title: Resume the Go legacy retirement plan from the current hierarchy trial
item.body:
The remaining Go hierarchy and member-family providers still use the legacy workspace index. Resume #7509 from the landed native trial and the successor session handoff, with a current service-path baseline and an executable path through correctness, cost acceptance, the provider switch and deletion.

The service baseline reproduces 392 missing legacy targets at 110 of 1,955 calls, with no native extras or false Complete answers and byte-identical observation controls. A reviewed scratch-only experiment removes duplicate preliminary proofs; its pilot preserves candidate discovery but recovers no target, exposing delayed projection after the family allowance stops. The full intervention and direct-subtype controls are running separately. Bare TestProject results are excluded from acceptance because explicit live-store inspection confirms the profile discrepancy tracked in #11198.

Coordinator 5992a212 reviewed Milestone 1 and the precise scratch-intervention plan before implementation. All diagnostic code stays on the never-merge branch `[redacted]`. Product fixes need review of measured results and their design; the existing owner hold on the production switch remains. This PR changes only the active plan.

Validation: source wiring, historical handoff and current constructor profiles checked; frozen public-answer controls recorded on #10588 and #11198. Diff checks and pack-authoring drift pass. No Rust test applies to the plan text.

Refs #7509, #10588, #9224, #11198.

- (b) Whether an override is a possible runtime target does not depend on abstractness at all. A concrete, non-final method can be overridden. Only a proof that it cannot be overridden (final, private, static, the existing `non_overridable`) removes overrides.

- proven abstract: overrides only. This is the #2580 behaviour.
- concrete: the external body, and overrides unless non-overridable.
- unknown: the same as concrete. It is the union, so it is the conservative answer.

#10985 M4 preparation: I am not the reviewer who made that ruling (it was session c43ff075), so this is my reading of messages 938 and 942 to 944, not a new ruling on the report contract.

Your proposal is consistent with the safety rules accepted there, and differs from that design in one point of scope.

Consistent:
- Item 2 of the accepted design says `finding_location_bound` is always unbounded for now, and that the bound is present exactly when further_findings_absent is partial. So a partial verdict with an unbounded location cannot support a local "no further findings", and abstaining on every undecided or partial unbounded case is the only sound scorer behaviour.
- Item 3 says M4 may qualify only `certified` enumeration. "Complete, certified, no omissions can qualify" is that.
- Rejecting a bounded variant that schema 7 cannot contain, and not fabricating bounds or adding a schema field, keeps the scorer honest about what the report says.

The difference: the same message says the bounded form (`procedures{..}`) "comes later, with M4". Your M4 does not deliver it; it defers partial-run qualification until an explicit bounded-location proof exists. That is a narrower M4 than the design anticipated. It is not unsound, but it changes what M4 gives a user: per-subject verdicts in a partial run stay informational, and nothing qualifies unless the run is complete and certified.

So: proceed with the scorer-only M4 as the safe core, drop the impossible synthetic bounded-positive expectation, and record the deferral in the plan with its reason. Tell the owner in your session that M4 will not qualify anything in a partial run until the bounded-location contract exists, because that is the benefit #10985 was aiming at and he may want the bounded form scheduled rather than left open. File the bounded-location work as its own issue so it is not lost.

Identity, for when you write it: if the scorer's result is stored anywhere (evaluation rows, a diff baseline's qualification metadata), a changed qualification for unchanged inputs needs a policy token; if it is computed per request from the report, it needs none. Cite which when you bring M4.

item.body:
`brokk-bifrost::suite_analyzers csharp_preprocessor_split_declarations_test::selected_configuration_readings_survive_identical_bytes_and_project_edits` fails on master 3ce4000bfa718005864e822955abb8ec9f1b9923 (run https://github.com/BrokkAi/bifrost-dev/actions/runs/42754686646, job 129635534268) at tests/suite_analyzers/../common/golden_case.rs:107 for tests/fixtures/golden/csharp-preprocessor/selected-configurations.

Decoded diff (expected left, actual right):
- disagreeing_owners and both `csharp_conditional_branch_unseen` obligation strings change from bare Project.csproj paths to `Feature/Feature.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]` and `Plain/Plain.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]`.
- The Shared.cs selected parse variant changes from dd256b9687ec0a30d808e12ba7b74ec4fb4c9a93bb1f91ad2da0c03699639ae6 to 577dd96af9599a7a02621fcfddd9e6a5d2a6946416c8fc82d4de2cb298b037ce.

#11223 (9ff290dc6c2119a44d89ac8391808ac2d5bcfa75, merged in batch #11249 at 3ce4000b) formats the C# owner key with its framework at crates/bifrost-store/src/analyzer/store/csharp_compilation.rs:1074; the fixture declares net10.0 at tests/suite_analyzers/csharp_preprocessor_split_declarations_test.rs:351-354. The expected file was not re-blessed, and batch #11249's validation did not run suite_analyzers.

Current origin/master 3f9d1b8e6ff6faf6ac51b3d862f6792d8186d0e1 still has the qualifier code and an expected file with no TargetFramework text, so this is deterministic and still present. #11230/#11237 cover only the three named-open usage-graph goldens; no repair touches this case.

Impact: the master Rust (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) job is red and blocks integration.

Next steps: audit the per-framework owner-key text and the changed Shared.cs parse variant, then re-bless tests/fixtures/golden/csharp-preprocessor/selected-configurations/expected.txt and run the suite_analyzers C# test. Do not reuse the named-open golden re-bless without checking these values.

### Triage evidence

The C# selected-configurations golden is stale after #11223 added `[TargetFramework=...]` to C# owner keys. Actual output now reports `Feature/Feature.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]` and `Plain/Plain.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]` in disagreement and obligation text, and produces a new Shared.cs parse variant; the expected file still has bare project paths and the old variant.

Run https://github.com/BrokkAi/bifrost-dev/actions/runs/42754686646, job 129635534268 (head 3ce4000bfa718005864e822955abb8ec9f1b9923), fails `brokk-bifrost::suite_analyzers csharp_preprocessor_split_declarations_test::selected_configuration_readings_survive_identical_bytes_and_project_edits` at tests/suite_analyzers/../common/golden_case.rs:107 for tests/fixtures/golden/csharp-preprocessor/selected-configurations. item.title: Master CI: C# selected-configurations golden is stale after #11223 adds TargetFramework owner keys
item.body:
`brokk-bifrost::suite_analyzers [redacted]::[redacted]` fails on master [redacted] (run https://github.com/BrokkAi/bifrost-dev/actions/runs/42754686646, job 129635534268) at tests/suite_analyzers/../common/golden_case.rs:107 for tests/fixtures/golden/csharp-preprocessor/[redacted]

Decoded diff (expected left, actual right):
- disagreeing_owners and both `[redacted]` obligation strings change from bare Project.csproj paths to `Feature/Feature.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]` and `Plain/Plain.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]`.
- The Shared.cs selected parse variant changes from [redacted] to [redacted]

#11223 ([redacted], merged in batch #11249 at 3ce4000b) formats the C# owner key with its framework at crates/bifrost-store/src/analyzer/store/csharp_compilation.rs:1074; the fixture declares net10.0 at tests/suite_analyzers/[redacted]:351-354. The expected file was not re-blessed, and batch #11249's validation did not run suite_analyzers.

Current origin/master [redacted] still has the qualifier code and an expected file with no TargetFramework text, so this is deterministic and still present. #11230/#11237 cover only the three named-open usage-graph goldens; no repair touches this case.

Impact: the master Rust ([redacted]) job is red and blocks integration.

Next steps: audit the per-framework owner-key text and the changed Shared.cs parse variant, then re-bless tests/fixtures/golden/csharp-preprocessor/selected-configurations/expected.txt and run the suite_analyzers C# test. Do not reuse the named-open golden re-bless without checking these values.

### Triage evidence

The C# selected-configurations golden is stale after #11223 added `[TargetFramework=...]` to C# owner keys. Actual output now reports `Feature/Feature.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]` and `Plain/Plain.csproj [TargetFramework=net10.0]` in disagreement and obligation text, and produces a new Shared.cs parse variant; the expected file still has bare project paths and the old variant.

Current origin/master [redacted] still has the qualifier code and an expected file with no TargetFramework text, so the mismatch is deterministic. Batch #11249 validation ran C# suite_semantic/issues/symbols/usages but not suite_analyzers. Issue #11230/PR #11237 cover only the three named-open usage-graph goldens; PR #11237's 30e0b952f4b additionally records Gamma's target framework in [redacted], but no repair touches csharp-preprocessor.

item.title: Java typestate: close analyzed dispatch families without proving a runtime target
item.body:
Java typestate cannot close a nonempty dispatch family even when its membership is exhaustively enumerated and every possible implementation closes the same subject. Each override correctly remains an Unproven may-target, but current summary projection and handoff composition fold that selection uncertainty into incomplete analysis. This is #11022 J2a part 2, dependent on #11148; #10497 has landed.

The Native-engine coordinator approved the parent design on 2026-11-10: a sealed dispatch membership witness proves the complete set, including absence of other overrides, then a protocol/subject-specific FamilyClosure is constructed only after every witnessed arm has complete bodies or exactly applicable reviewed summaries, candidate-local bindings, subject continuity, and normal/exceptional effect coverage. Keep individual may-target proof and taint witnesses unchanged; factor selection weakness from independent binding/effect weakness before conjunction.

Preserve #2277 literally: concrete expansion OFF stays census-only/open for nonempty families; ON and mandatory #2580 interface/abstract discovery may close after all-arm analysis. Unknown artifact kind, incomplete hierarchy/source-JAR families, missing bodies, partial summaries, conversion effects, budget/cancellation and binding gaps remain open. No new workspace-wide derivation or cache, SQL certificate, adapter/IR/schema change, or product-pack authoring.

Acceptance uses one product golden for all-closing, mixed closing/leaking, exceptional-only leak and incomplete controls, including external Base -> Parent plus a workspace override. A real cached-root add-override mutation must invalidate the former complete family through its membership read key/digest even though all old members and root bytes are unchanged. Cold/warm and summary-hit receipts must agree. The first behavior PR may keep bounded snapshot mode explicitly incomplete; its follow-up and parity control must prevent a clean absence claim there.

Coordinator identity ruling: rotate both ICFG domains; append the issue-specific java-family-closure policy component. No protocol domain is needed if ProductionTypestateSummaryStorage remains process-local only; cite the owner/lifetime in the PR. Final numbered literals are set strictly above master at submission. Implementation starts on a new branch from the exact submitted #11148 head after the full ExecPlan is committed.

item.title: Java typestate: close analyzed dispatch families without proving a runtime target
item.body:
Java typestate cannot close a nonempty dispatch family even when its membership is exhaustively enumerated and every possible implementation closes the same subject. Each override correctly remains an Unproven may-target, but current summary projection and handoff composition fold that selection uncertainty into incomplete analysis. This is #11022 J2a part 2, dependent on #11148; #10497 has landed.

The Native-engine coordinator approved the parent design on 2026-11-10: a sealed dispatch membership witness proves the complete set, including absence of other overrides, then a protocol/subject-specific FamilyClosure is constructed only after every witnessed arm has complete bodies or exactly applicable reviewed summaries, candidate-local bindings, subject continuity, and normal/exceptional effect coverage. Keep individual may-target proof and taint witnesses unchanged; factor selection weakness from independent binding/effect weakness before conjunction.

Preserve #2277 literally: concrete expansion OFF stays census-only/open for nonempty families; ON and mandatory #2580 interface/abstract discovery may close after all-arm analysis. Unknown artifact kind, incomplete hierarchy/source-JAR families, missing bodies, partial summaries, conversion effects, budget/cancellation and binding gaps remain open. No new workspace-wide derivation or cache, SQL certificate, adapter/IR/schema change, or product-pack authoring.

Acceptance uses one product golden for all-closing, mixed closing/leaking, exceptional-only leak and incomplete controls, including external Base -> Parent plus a workspace override. A real cached-root add-override mutation must invalidate the former complete family through its membership read key/digest even though all old members and root bytes are unchanged. Cold/warm and summary-hit receipts must agree. The first behavior PR may keep bounded snapshot mode explicitly incomplete; its follow-up and parity control must prevent a clean absence claim there.

Coordinator identity ruling: rotate both ICFG domains; append the issue-specific java-family-closure policy component. No protocol domain is needed if [redacted] remains process-local only; cite the owner/lifetime in the PR. Final numbered literals are set strictly above master at submission. Implementation starts on a new branch from the exact submitted #11148 head after the full ExecPlan is committed.

item.title: TUI keeps delivered messages pinned as Queued below the conversation
item.body:
Delivered user messages can remain pinned as `Queued` below the TUI conversation. These local rows obscure newer replies. Reopening the conversation clears them.

Investigate authoritative submission reconciliation and the event-loop paths that keep warm conversations current, particularly under sustained background updates. Fix the state/update ownership and add a regression that verifies delivered rows disappear; hiding the status label alone is insufficient.

Investigation: the worker queue and durable transcript can be correct while the TUI retains local pending rows. The command identities agree, so this is not an actual unsent-message queue. No direct submission-renderer change was found in the reported day's commits. Fresh isolated TUI sends, a large terminal, a normal daemon reconnect, and a TUI paused through a completed turn all retired the local rows correctly. A combined paused-client/restart experiment timed out during restart and gives no verdict on queued-row behavior.

The triggering state was cleared by reopening. No speculative code fix has been made; inspect a still-affected live pane when the problem recurs, particularly its pending submissions and the authoritative snapshots applied to that same chat/composer owner.

3. **Uses.** Which operations take, reuse or need a checkpoint: suspend, resume, move, destroy, discard, upgrades, and retention.

- **Retention (confirmed).** Each session keeps one current archive. When a new one is saved, the old one is deleted, unless an active Move still needs it (`staging.rs:544-567`).
- **Worker upgrades (confirmed).** Upgrades don't take checkpoints. They wait until the worker is idle. The container upgrade path says so directly: "no checkpoint or worker-root reset is involved" (`container_upgrade.rs:29-31`).

Agent: `staging.rs:435` runs a full structural check on an installed archive. That may affect the mismatch claim, so I'll look at when it runs.
Agent: A Mjolnir checkpoint is a ZIP archive of one session that the daemon keeps on its own host. Each archive covers the session up to an exact point in the worker's journal. It holds the conversation and queued work, the Git state of each project repository, and a fixed list of the harness's own session files.

The worker's journal protects work while the target still exists. A checkpoint lets Mjolnir rebuild the session on a new target after the old one is gone. Suspend, Resume, Move and recovery after a lost target all depend on it.

## Two layers of durability

- **Journal (on the target).** The worker records every command and event before it acknowledges them. The journal survives daemon restarts, but it is lost if the target is lost.
- **Checkpoint archive (on the controller).** Stored as `data_dir/sessions/<session>-<frontier>-<archive-id>.hel.zip`. The "frontier" is the journal position it covers, recorded as a number plus a digest.
- **How they connect.** The worker may delete journal history only up to `min(acknowledged_through, recovery_floor_ordinal)` (`mj-core/src/relay/snapshot.rs:1735`):
  - `acknowledged_through` is how far the daemon has saved events to its database.
  - `recovery_floor_ordinal` is how far a saved checkpoint covers. It moves only after a verified archive is recorded in the database.

## What an archive contains

- **Format** (`mj-checkpoint/src/archive.rs:27-40`):
  - A ZIP file. Small metadata uses DEFLATE; large payloads use Zstandard and are split into 16 MiB parts so they can be compressed and checked in parallel.
  - Limits: 8 MiB for the manifest, 8 GiB per payload, 32 GiB per archive.
- **`manifest.json`.** Describes the session, target, bundle and versions, and lists each payload's SHA-256, size and file mode. The target description must not contain credentials (`mj-core/src/archive.rs:77-82`).

A Mjolnir checkpoint is a ZIP archive of one session that the daemon keeps on its own host. Each archive covers the session up to an exact point in the worker's journal. It holds the conversation and queued work, the Git state of each project repository, and a fixed list of the harness's own session files.

The worker's journal protects work while the target still exists. A checkpoint lets Mjolnir rebuild the session on a new target after the old one is gone. Suspend, Resume, Move and recovery after a lost target all depend on it.

## Two layers of durability

- **Journal (on the target).** The worker records every command and event before it acknowledges them. The journal survives daemon restarts, but it is lost if the target is lost.
- **Checkpoint archive (on the controller).** Stored as `data_dir/sessions/<session>-<frontier>-<archive-id>.hel.zip`. The "frontier" is the journal position it covers, recorded as a number plus a digest.
- **How they connect.** The worker may delete journal history only up to `min(acknowledged_through, recovery_floor_ordinal)` (`mj-core/src/relay/snapshot.rs:1735`):
  - `acknowledged_through` is how far the daemon has saved events to its database.
  - `recovery_floor_ordinal` is how far a saved checkpoint covers. It moves only after a verified archive is recorded in the database.

## What an archive contains

- **Format** (`mj-checkpoint/src/archive.rs:27-40`):
  - A ZIP file. Small metadata uses DEFLATE; large payloads use Zstandard and are split into 16 MiB parts so they can be compressed and checked in parallel.
  - Limits: 8 MiB for the manifest, 8 GiB per payload, 32 GiB per archive.
- **`manifest.json`.** Describes the session, target, bundle and versions, and lists each payload's SHA-256, size and file mode. The target description must not contain credentials (`mj-core/src/archive.rs:77-82`).
- **`canonical/session.json`.** The transcript and session state at the frontier, plus queued prompts and queued configuration changes. On restore this sets up the worker's relay state; it is not replayed into the harness (`restore.rs:110-116`).
- **Each repository** (`archive.rs:42-61`):
  - a Git bundle of committed work;
  - binary patches for staged and unstaged changes;
  - a tar of untracked files (ignored files are left out);
  - conflict and state files if a merge or rebase is in progress.
- **Repository rules:**
  - Origins with embedded credentials are removed or rejected.
  - Dirty submodules are refused (`checkpoint/submodules.rs:44-109`).
  - A bundle can be "thin": it depends on commits the remote must still have. That is checked before restore.
- **Harness files.** Each harness has an allowlist of native session files (`native_scan.rs:467-479`). Credentials are not archived; the profile supplies them again on resume. A Codex goal and its budget are exported separately (`mj-worker/src/checkpoint/codex_goal.rs`).
- **Not included:** anything outside the project workspace. That means installed packages, the rest of the home directory, `/tmp`, container layers, and plain directories that are not Git repositories (`archive/git.rs:241-244`).

## How a checkpoint is taken

1. **Request.** A request comes from the CLI, the automatic scheduler, Suspend or Move. The daemon records an owner for the operation, and it refuses a second lifecycle operation on the same session at the same time (`controller/checkpoint/capture.rs:59-76`).
2. **Quiet check.** The session must have no active turn or tool, queued prompt, terminal, background command, active Codex goal, or unknown provider state (`mj-core/src/activity.rs:704-774`). If the session is busy, a routine checkpoint waits and tries again later; this is not recorded as a failure.
3. **Barrier.** The worker finishes earlier commands and turns, then stops starting new agent work. It reports the exact journal position (`mj-worker/src/relay/commands.rs:1108-1136`). If a new turn, question or goal starts during the hold, the hold ends and the attempt is dropped (`relay/checkpoint_hold.rs`).
4. **Latch.** The daemon checks that its own database has reached exactly that journal position, then takes exclusive use of the worker connection (`latched.rs:464-531`). If the current archive's content still matches the session, it reuses that archive instead of building a new one (`staging.rs:418`).
5. **Capture, then release.** The session state is copied into a staging area on the target. For a routine checkpoint the worker then resumes agent work before the archive is packed and transferred, so the pause is short. Suspend keeps the pause in place until the session is closed (`latched.rs:587-665`).
6. **Transfer.** The archive is copied by local copy, container copy, or SSH. The daemon hashes the bytes it received and compares that with the target's SHA-256. It then renames the file into place, restricts its permissions and syncs the directory (`checkpoint_transfer.rs:150-189`).
7. **Publish.** One database transaction replaces the session's `session_checkpoints` row; the automatic path only replaces it if nothing else changed it first. The old archive is then deleted, unless a Move still needs it (`staging.rs:544-567`).
8. **Advance the recovery floor.** The daemon tells the worker the new floor, and the worker may then delete journal history up to it. If this message fails, the archive is still valid; the worker just keeps more history than it needs to.

## When checkpoints are taken

- **Automatically** (`mj-controller/src/recovery.rs`):
  - When the session is idle, has a completed turn newer than its archive, and the archive is at least 10 minutes old. The first eligible turn is captured without waiting.
  - Each attempt has a 15-minute time limit.
  - After a failure, it retries after 10 minutes, doubling up to 2 hours.
  - If the session is busy, it tries again after 30 seconds, doubling up to 10 minutes.
- **Manually:** `mj checkpoint --session <id>`. The API's bundle export also takes one (`server_runtime/api.rs:2278-2306`).
- **As part of Suspend and Move.**

## How checkpoints are used

| Operation | How it uses the checkpoint |
|---|---|
| Suspend | Records the intent first, takes a new archive or reuses a verified one, saves it, closes the worker's relay, then removes the target (`lifecycle.rs:260-559`). If the checkpoint fails, the target is kept. |
| Daemon restart during Suspend | If the relay was already closed, uses the saved archive. If not, takes a new one, because the saved one may be out of date (`lifecycle.rs:570-581`). |
| Resume | Fully verifies the archive, restores it on a new target, supplies credentials again, and asks whether to start or discard queued work (`resume.rs:1180-1204`, `:1613-1651`). |
| Move | Restores from the checkpoint. A same-target move keeps the environment and replaces only the harness. A move to a different harness also creates a summary of the transcript for the new harness (`move_session.rs`, `handoff.rs:71-104`). On failure, the session stops and keeps the checkpoint. |
| Discard changes since checkpoint | Uses the existing archive without taking a new one (`daemon/resume.rs:160-193`). |
| Destroy | Deletes every archive for the session (`checkpoint/archives.rs:113-160`). |
| SessionWiki, publication | Read and verify archives; they do not create them (`sessionwiki.rs:293`, `publication.rs:283`). |
| Worker and container upgrades | Do not use checkpoints. They wait until the worker is idle (`controller/container_upgrade.rs:29-31`). |

**Retention.** Each session keeps one current archive. At startup, the daemon deletes archives that no database record refers to (`checkpoint/archives.rs:3-68`).

## The docs claim more verification than the code does

`docs/src/content/docs/durability.md:97-101` says that after transfer the daemon checks the archive's structure and each payload hash. That is not true for a newly taken archive:

- After transfer, the daemon checks only the SHA-256 of the whole file (`checkpoint_transfer.rs:153-171`).
- The export code says this is deliberate: full structural checks happen "on resume/import" (`mj-checkpoint/src/checkpoint/capture.rs:739-742`).
- The check before Suspend removes the target, `verify_installed_checkpoint_gate`, is also SHA-only (`staging.rs:479-494`).
- Full checks (`verify_archive_streaming`) run on Resume, Move, reuse of an existing archive, and publication.

**Likely effect:** a Suspend that takes a new archive can remove the target without ever reading that archive back. The SHA check catches damage during transfer. It does not catch a bug in the code that writes the archive. Such a bug would show up only at Resume, after the target is gone.

**Recommendation:** at least correct the doc. Also consider adding a full check, only in Suspend and Move just before the target is removed. Routine checkpoints can stay hash-only, because the target remains and the previous archive is untouched. The cost is reading the archive once more on the daemon's host, up to 32 GiB.

**Evidence.** I read these parts of the code myself: the archive format, schema versions, retention, the journal deletion rule, the transfer hash check and the check before teardown. The barrier and latch steps, quiet rules, scheduling times, restore steps and harness allowlists come from the three read-only child reports, which cite line references. I did not run anything.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The worker keeps journal history until two separate conditions hold: the database has the events (`acknowledged_through`), and a saved checkpoint covers them (the recovery floor). Either one alone could lose work, because the database copy does not help rebuild a target and an archive is not trusted until it is saved.
- A routine checkpoint lets the agent continue before the archive is transferred, while the recovery floor waits for the saved archive. So the pause is short, and journal history is never deleted for an archive that might still fail.
- Each archive declares the lowest schema version its content needs (`mj-core/src/archive.rs:16-22`). Small archives stay readable by older builds, and older builds refuse newer content with a clear version error instead of misreading it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

item.title: TUI keeps delivered messages pinned as Queued below the conversation
item.body:
Delivered user messages can remain pinned as `Queued` below the TUI conversation. These local rows obscure newer replies. Reopening the conversation clears them.

Investigate authoritative submission reconciliation and the event-loop paths that keep warm conversations current, particularly under sustained background updates. Fix the state/update ownership and add a regression that verifies delivered rows disappear; hiding the status label alone is insufficient.

Investigation: the worker queue and durable transcript can be correct while the TUI retains local pending rows. The command identities agree, so this is not an actual unsent-message queue. No direct submission-renderer change was found in the reported day's commits. Fresh isolated TUI sends, a large terminal, a normal daemon reconnect, and a TUI paused through a completed turn all retired the local rows correctly. A combined paused-client/restart experiment timed out during restart and gives no verdict on queued-row behavior.

The triggering state was cleared by reopening. No speculative code fix has been made; inspect a still-affected live pane when the problem recurs, particularly its pending submissions and the authoritative snapshots applied to that same chat/composer owner.

item.title: Use the key saved in DSH before the environment and Mjolnir secrets
item.body:
A DSH profile refused to start unless `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` was exported or set in the profile's `environment`, even when the person had saved a key in DSH itself:

> worker bootstrap failed: profile "dsh": DSH authenticates with DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, which is set neither in the environment Mjolnir started with nor under [profiles.dsh.environment] …

DSH keeps that key under `refs` in `<DSH home>/.credentials.yaml` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-credentials-local` in [deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness)).

## What changes

A DSH profile's key is decided once, as the configuration is read; first found wins:

1. the key saved in DSH: `refs.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in `.credentials.yaml` in the profile home (DSH's home, `~/.dsh` by default);
2. `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in the environment Mjolnir started with;
3. `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in the DSH home's `.env`;
4. the profile's own `environment` entry, such as a `secrets.toml` secret.

The first three are DSH's own precedence, so a session uses the key `dsh` uses. Doctor, Setup, session start and utility inference all read the one resolved environment.

- The store is read as DSH reads it: `version: 1` or the flat layout DSH migrates, strict `refs`, and a refusal with `chmod 600` when other users can read the file (DSH refuses it too).
- The `.env` reader matches Node's `util.parseEnv`, which DSH uses.
- A DeepSeek account browser sign-in is recognized but not used: DSH sends it as `x-dsh-auth-token` to its Messages endpoint, while dsh-acp sends only a bearer API key. The refusal says so instead of reporting the key as missing.
- New dependency: `yaml-rust2` (MIT/Apache-2.0); the workspace had no YAML parser.

## Validation

- `cargo test` for mj-core, mj-controller, mj-tui and mj-cli; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`.
- New tests: the precedence order including the sign-in and permission refusals (fails on the old code), and `.env` parity with Node 22's `util.parseEnv`.
- Real `mj doctor` in an isolated `--instance`: a saved key reports ready; no key names every place checked; a 0644 store gets the `chmod 600` refusal.

It does one useful thing, and it causes the trap you just hit. I think your skepticism is mostly right, but I'd change how the check works rather than delete it outright.

**Why it was added.** The 2026-09-13 plan (`.agents/plans/mjolnir-subagent-toolset.md`, decision log line 44) set up checkboxes for "additional eligible profile IDs," with the parent's own profile always eligible so it "works without initial setup." Back then a parent picked a profile and model for each child. The list limited what a parent could pick. Since then, spawn stopped taking a profile or model (`docs/.../api-reference.md:485`). There is now one global model per task type, and Mjolnir picks the profile by remaining quota.

**What it still does.** It keeps sub-agents from drawing on certain accounts. Examples: a pay-per-token API profile, or a subscription you want to save for your own sessions. That would matter when two profiles offer the same model ID. The quota ranking would then choose between them, and the review docs say API billing counts as "healthy" quota (`turn-review.md:19`). If sub-agent ranking works the same way, which is likely but I haven't checked, an API-billed profile could win over a subscription that is running low. I also don't know whether any of your API profiles (openrouter, glm, deepseek) share model IDs with your subscription profiles.

**Why it breaks your config.** The settings form ignores the list on purpose. `take_setup_subagent_choices` (`mj-tui/src/setup.rs:2374`) marks every enabled profile eligible before it builds the model picker. Its comment says: "A global picker sees every enabled installation, rather than one parent's eligibility." So the form offered `grok-4.7`, and the move check, which does apply the list, rejected it.

Syncing the form can't fully fix this. The parent's own profile is always eligible, so whether a choice is valid depends on which session is the parent. With your current list, `opus` works for a Claude parent but fails for a Codex parent. A global setting combined with a per-parent allowlist will always be valid for some sessions and not others.

**My recommendation:** change the allowlist to an opt-out. Every enabled profile is eligible unless you mark it "Exclude from sub-agents." That removes the trap, makes the form and the move check agree for every parent, and keeps the one real use. Under your compatibility preference, old configs keep loading: an existing `eligible_profiles` list would be read as "everything not listed is excluded," so current behavior doesn't change unless you choose to switch.

If you don't care about the API-billing case, removing the list entirely is simpler and also reasonable.

For now, adding `grok = true` under `[subagents.eligible_profiles]` unblocks the move. I haven't changed anything.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The bug comes from two settings with different scopes. The model is a global setting. Eligibility is "the list plus whoever the parent is," so it varies by session. Any check that compares them can only be right for some parents.
- The form's comment shows that someone saw this mismatch and chose the broad picker. That fixed "the picker shows too few models" but moved the failure to launch and move time.
- An opt-out makes the default safe in both directions. New profiles are usable right away, and an exclusion is a choice you make on purpose rather than something you get by forgetting a checkbox.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

- **Old configs:** a config that still has `[subagents.eligible_profiles]` loads without error. The key is ignored and is dropped the next time the config is saved. The config version is unchanged.

- **Updated:** the docs, the skill reference, the spawn tool description, and the doctor wording. They now say "enabled profile."

**Cause:** the session's saved state kept the full text of its last 512 finished commands, and a second copy of each in `dispatches`. Messages that carry child reports can be about 29 KB each. That passed the 16 MiB limit, so the worker could no longer save its state and failed every restart.

**What changed (`31ccf03cd`):**
- **Finished commands are kept in short form.** Each one keeps a SHA-256 digest, its mailbox event key, and three flags. Their duplicate records are deleted. Queued and running commands still keep their full text. A retried command with the same ID still gets its original result, and a different command reusing that ID is still refused.
- **The file is written without indentation.** The size limit is checked on the bytes that are actually written.
- **Old oversized files can be recovered.** On start, the worker reads an older file up to 64 MiB, shrinks it, and saves it under 16 MiB.
- **State format version 19 → 20,** following the repo's rule for this kind of shape change.

I checked the code paths that read these records myself:
- Retry matching (`commands.rs:315`)

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The worker already limited how many finished commands it kept. Nothing limited how many bytes they took. A count limit only bounds size if each item is small, and child-report messages are not.
- A retry only needs to know whether it is the same command. A digest answers that without keeping the text. Mailbox events are matched by event key instead, because an older worker may have stored the plain-text version of the same event.

**It hit a time limit; nothing cancelled it on purpose.** The first restart attempt ran out of its 30-second limit. It failed safely, and the next attempt 41 seconds later worked.

**What the new daemon's log shows (confirmed):**
- **16:55:33.896:** "relay worker is unreachable; probing it before recovery" (line 128). The restart attempt starts.
- **16:56:03.947:** "replace stale relay worker launch config: operation cancelled" (line 170). This is 30.05 seconds later. At the same moment, the cleanup of the half-staged worker binary also reports "operation cancelled" (line 169).
- **16:56:44:** the second attempt starts (line 490), after the 60-second cooldown.
- **16:57:12–13:** the worker starts. The queued child-finished message is accepted, and `relay-state.json` is rewritten at 451 KB, down from 16.7 MB.

**Why the message says "cancelled" (confirmed from code):** automatic recovery runs its commands through `CancellableProcessExecutor::with_timeout(WORKER_RESTART_TIMEOUT)`, and that timeout is 30 seconds (`mj-controller/src/session_manager.rs:47`, `recovery.rs:142`). When the time limit passes, `is_cancelled()` returns true (`mj-core/src/targets.rs:1021`), so the command fails with "operation cancelled". Nothing else stopped it.

**Why it took more than 30 seconds (likely, not verified):** after an upgrade, the stale-launch-config step also stages a copy of the new 52 MB worker binary into the session's worker directory. It did this while the daemon was still starting up. That period had database writes of 2–7 seconds (`store_catalog_project` 6.9 s, `record_api_activities` 2.9 s), and other sessions were going through the same restart. I did not measure which step used the time.

**Current state:** `e6e79de5` is running on the new build. The status line no longer says "no harness activity", and the child report it was waiting for has been delivered.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The word "cancelled" here really means the time limit ran out. When the cause is a timeout, saying "timed out after 30 s" in the error would have made this obvious from the log line alone.
- The first restart after an upgrade does more work than a normal restart, because it copies a new worker binary. A 30-second limit is fine for a normal restart but can be too short for that first one when the daemon is busy starting up. The 60-second cooldown hid the cost here.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Two things to note:**
1. **Most of the 15-minute wait was my mistake.** My earlier `mj sessions … | head -3` killed the new-build client while the old daemon was still waiting to hand over. That stopped the handoff until I ran the command again without `head`. After that, the handoff took about 20 seconds.
2. **Possible follow-up (not done):** report time-limit failures as "timed out after 30 s", or give the first restart after an upgrade more time. Tell me if you want either one.

I checked the code. There is no gradual decay. A provider failure puts a temporary on/off mark on the profile and model, and the mark ends at a set time. 400-class errors other than 429 and 402 are never recorded.

**What gets a mark** (`ProfileFault::of`, `mj-controller/src/profile_health.rs:36`):
- 429, or the Codex code `limit`: rate-limited.
- 402, or a usage-limit diagnostic: out of quota.
- 500, 502, 503, 504, 529, or the Codex code `service`: provider error.
- Any other 4xx, such as 400, 401 or 403, gets no mark. The comment at the top of the file says a malformed request is the request's fault, not the profile's. Refused logins are handled separately by `RejectedLogins`.

**How long a mark lasts** (`ProfileHealth::record`, line 105):
- The first failure marks the profile and model for 60 seconds (`BASE_BACKOFF`).
- If it fails again within 10 minutes after the last mark ended (`QUIET_RESET`), the strike count goes up and the backoff doubles: 60 s, 120 s, 240 s, and so on, up to 15 minutes (`MAX_BACKOFF`).
- After 10 minutes with no failure since the mark ended, the count starts again at 60 seconds. This is the only "decay" in the system: a reset to the start after a quiet period.
- Failures that arrive while a mark is still active do not lengthen it. The reasoning is that several sessions that started before the mark all failing together is one event.
- If the provider sends a reset time (`reset_at`, as RFC 3339 or epoch seconds or milliseconds), that time is used instead of the computed backoff.

**How selection uses the mark** (`mj-controller/src/server/api/subagents.rs:486` and `:256`):
- A marked candidate is skipped, not ranked lower. Spawn takes the first candidate that offers the model and has no active mark.
- If every candidate is marked, spawn returns an error that lists each mark (`all_unhealthy`).
- The remaining-quota percentage (`remaining_percent`) is a separate input to selection. Health marks do not change it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The marks are stored only in memory, in a static (`profile_health::shared()`, a `OnceLock<Mutex<…>>`). A daemon restart clears all of them.
- Marks are keyed by (profile, model), not by profile alone. One model failing at the provider does not stop the same account from serving another model.
- Expired marks stay in the map. `unhealthy()` filters them out by time instead of deleting them, so the old entry is still there to count strikes when the next failure arrives.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

If you want a score that decays gradually instead of an on/off mark, this would need new code. Today's design only switches a profile off for a while. Tell me if you want to discuss options.

Short answer: the shape is right, and I would keep it. It is a circuit breaker, not a load balancer, and for a handful of profiles that is the correct tool. The weak points are in the details, not the shape.

**What I think is right**

- On/off marks beat a decaying score here. With three or four profiles, a weighted score adds tuning constants and makes "why did spawn pick this profile" hard to explain in the error text. The current `all_unhealthy` message can say "rate-limited until 14:05 UTC" because the state is a single timestamp.
- Keying by (profile, model) matches how providers actually throttle.
- Not extending a mark while it is active is correct. Ten children that all started before the throttle and all fail together are one event.
- Honouring `reset_at` when the provider gives it is the best signal available and the code prefers it.
- Leaving 400, 401 and 403 unmarked is correct. Those are the request's fault or the login's fault, and `RejectedLogins` already owns the login case.

**What I would change**

1. Success never heals a mark. `ProfileHealth` has `record` and `unhealthy` and nothing else (confirmed from the file: no clear method). Sessions already running on a marked profile keep taking turns. If one of them succeeds, the provider is serving that account again, and the mark should end. Today the only way out is the clock. This matters because the alternative probe is expensive: a spawn after the mark ends is a real child, and if it fails the parent has to close it and respawn. Existing sessions are free probes and the design throws their evidence away.

2. One 5xx is a weak signal; one 429 is a strong one. The code treats them the same: one 503 takes the profile out for 60 seconds. A 429 means the account is throttled, so skipping it is right. A single 503 among many concurrent successes is usually noise. I would either require two provider errors within a short window before marking, or make the first 5xx backoff shorter than the first 429 backoff. I would not add a success counter or error rate; that is the weighted score I argued against above.

3. Quota exhaustion without `reset_at` caps at 15 minutes. An exhausted plan resets in hours or at a week boundary, so the cap means a failing spawn every 15 minutes, each one a child the parent must clean up. Two options: a much longer cap for `QuotaExhausted` specifically, or let the quota poller lift and set these marks. The poller already tracks `rate_limited_until_epoch_seconds` per profile (`mj-controller/src/quota.rs:360`), so the daemon has a second, cheaper source of truth that `ProfileHealth` does not consult.

4. In-memory only. This is fine. Marks are at most 15 minutes and a restart that clears them costs one failed spawn at worst. Not worth persisting.

**Recommendation**

Keep the on/off design. Do item 1 first; it is small, it uses evidence the daemon already has, and it removes the most user-visible cost (failed probe spawns). Item 3 is next if quota exhaustion without a reset time happens in practice; I do not know how often providers omit `reset_at`, and that is worth checking in the stored diagnostics before building anything. Item 2 is a judgement call and I would wait for evidence that single 5xx marks are actually causing avoidable skips.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This is the classic closed / open / half-open circuit breaker, minus half-open. In the textbook version the half-open state lets one request through as a probe. Here the probe is a full child spawn, which is why using existing sessions' successes as the probe is the natural fit for this codebase.
- The strike counter only advances on a failure within `QUIET_RESET` after the previous mark ended. Because spawns are skipped during the mark, that failure almost always comes from a new child spawned right after the mark ends. So the doubling is really "the probe failed again", which is the right thing to escalate on.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I pushed items 1 and 2 to master as `3ab24f3e2`.

**What changed**
- **5xx backoff:** a provider error now skips the profile for 8 s, then 16 s, 32 s and 64 s, and stays at 64 s after that. Rate limits and exhausted quota are unchanged: 60 s, doubling up to 15 min.
- **A success clears the mark:** when a turn completes on a marked profile and model, the mark and its strike count are removed. This only happens if the turn completed after the mark was set, so a session catching up on old events can't clear a new mark.

A child wrote the first version. I made two fixes to it:
- **Bug:** a success only cleared marks while some mark was still active. A success shortly after a mark ended was ignored, so the next failure still doubled the backoff instead of starting at 60 s. The check now also covers marks in their 10-minute quiet window, and I added a test for this case.
- **Readability:** each observation is now a small `TurnHealth` enum (failed or succeeded) instead of a tuple of two `Option`s where only one could be set. `ProfileHealth::observe` handles both cases.

**Tests:** all 6 `profile_health` tests pass, and clippy (`--all-targets`, `-D warnings`) and fmt are clean. There is no test for the new success handling in `standalone.rs`, because that file has no test helpers to build one on. Clippy compiles it, but no test runs it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The mark is set at the time the event is processed, but a success uses the time it was recorded. If a failure and a success arrive in the same batch of events, the success looks older and doesn't clear the mark. That leans towards skipping a profile a little too long, which is the safer mistake.
- Removing the mark entirely on success, instead of shortening it, also keeps the map from growing.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Item 3 is not done yet.** The plan: when quota runs out, end the mark at the reset time that autocontinue already works out (`recovery_reset` plus quota windows), with no 15-minute cap. If no reset time is known, keep the current backoff. Tell me if you want it.

item.title: Use the key saved in DSH before the environment and Mjolnir secrets
item.body:
A DSH profile refused to start unless `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` was exported or set in the profile's `environment`, even when the person had saved a key in DSH itself:

> worker bootstrap failed: profile "dsh": DSH authenticates with DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, which is set neither in the environment Mjolnir started with nor under [[redacted]] …

DSH keeps that key under `refs` in `<DSH home>/.credentials.yaml` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-credentials-local` in [deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness)).

## What changes

A DSH profile's key is decided once, as the configuration is read; first found wins:

1. the key saved in DSH: `refs.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in `.credentials.yaml` in the profile home (DSH's home, `~/.dsh` by default);
2. `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in the environment Mjolnir started with;
3. `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in the DSH home's `.env`;
4. the profile's own `environment` entry, such as a `secrets.toml` secret.

The first three are DSH's own precedence, so a session uses the key `dsh` uses. Doctor, Setup, session start and utility inference all read the one resolved environment.

- The store is read as DSH reads it: `version: 1` or the flat layout DSH migrates, strict `refs`, and a refusal with `chmod 600` when other users can read the file (DSH refuses it too).
- The `.env` reader matches Node's `util.parseEnv`, which DSH uses.
- A DeepSeek account browser sign-in is recognized but not used: DSH sends it as `x-dsh-auth-token` to its Messages endpoint, while dsh-acp sends only a bearer API key. The refusal says so instead of reporting the key as missing.
- New dependency: `yaml-rust2` (MIT/Apache-2.0); the workspace had no YAML parser.

## Validation

item.title: Keep Codex mailbox delivery at turn boundaries (#1277)
item.body:
## Summary

Fixes #1277.

The worker installs a Codex `PostToolUse` hook that drains the session mailbox mid-turn and injects events as `additionalContext`. Codex records that context as a developer message **between** a `function_call` and its `function_call_output` in the rollout. DeepSeek's chat API rejects any history holding a tool call not immediately followed by its output, so a single mid-turn mailbox delivery permanently poisoned the stored conversation — every subsequent request failed with `No tool output found for tool call`, killing 8 of 10 lanes in Series 37. OpenAI's API tolerates the ordering, which is why only the DeepSeek profile died.

- The relay now answers `PostToolUse` drains empty and never leases mailbox events to them. mj cannot observe Codex's internal recording order, so no relay-side predicate can make mid-turn hook injection safe; the structural fix is turn-boundary delivery only.
- Codex sessions still get timely delivery: wake events (review verdicts, child reports, parent/session messages) start a mailbox wake turn as soon as the relay is quiet, and non-wake events attach to the next prompt, exactly as before for the non-hook paths.
- The hook stays installed as a harmless probe, so staged profiles and mixed-version workers keep working unchanged.
- Claude's `PostToolBatch` delivery, including hook steering, is untouched.

Already-poisoned sessions still cannot be repaired from the client side; the issue's optional ask (2) — detect-and-repair on `mj prompt` — is left as a follow-up.

## Test plan

- New hard-won regression test `relay::tests::mailbox_post_tool_use_drains_stay_empty_and_leave_events_for_turn_boundaries`: a `PostToolUse` drain returns empty, creates no lease, and leaves events pending; a `PostToolBatch` drain then delivers them.
- New end-to-end test `mailbox_post_tool_use_hook_stays_empty_and_turn_boundaries_deliver` in `mj-worker/tests/mailbox_hook.rs`: real hook binary over a real control socket.
- Existing hook drain/lease/ack/replay tests switched to `PostToolBatch` (same coverage of the machinery).
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; full `brokk-mj-worker` suite green; full `brokk-mj-controller` suite green except `server::tests::settings_routes_hide_literal_secrets_and_save_through_the_shared_model`, which fails identically on unmodified master in this environment.

{"conversation": "Agent: I agree. A busy host should make a child start slowly, not fail. The cause is a fixed deadline.

## What happened

- **The deadline.** Before a worker starts, it runs your login shell interactively (`bash -l -i -c …`) to read the session environment. That probe has a fixed limit, `DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT = 10s` (`mj-core/src/login_environment.rs:121`). It was added on 2026-10-22 in `17384dbde`, "Read the session environment from an interactive login shell".
- **Why it ran out.** At load 260–300, from the bifrost test suites, starting bash took longer than 10 seconds. The worker exited without publishing its control socket.
- **No retry.** Spawn records that as a permanent failure. A child in error can't be sent a message, and in this case it can't even be closed. `close` fails because it tries to recover a worker that has no socket.

The comment above the constant gives the reason for the deadline: a startup file that waits for input shouldn't hang a session. But a fixed limit can't tell "waiting for input" apart from "slow because the machine is busy".

## What I'd change

1. **Remove the reason for a short deadline.** Run the probe with stdin from `/dev/null`, so a startup file that reads input gets end-of-file and continues. A long limit, for example 2 minutes, then only catches startup files that are truly stuck, such as one waiting on a network mount. The csh path sends its script on stdin, so it needs its own handling.
2. **Retry startup timeouts in spawn** before reporting failure. A slow host should show up as a slow child, not an error.
3. **Make `close` work on a child whose worker never started.** There's nothing to recover in that case, so close should just settle the record.

**Short answer:** Yes. The rule I'd use is that the agent never decides that its own change is trivial, because that judgment is what the review checks. The agent always calls `request_review`. Mjolnir then decides whether a reviewer is needed, using one of two kinds of rule:

1. A fact that Mjolnir can check in Git: the pushed tree contains nothing that hasn't already been reviewed or published.
2. A path rule that you write in the configuration.

The agent's workflow stays the same. Sometimes the clean verdict just arrives at once. The pre-push hook stays a simple check for `refs/mj/reviewed/<tree>` (`mj-worker/src/review/hook.rs:26`).

## Why merges are expensive today (confirmed)

In `capture_pushable_commits` (`mj-worker/src/review/capture.rs:266-297`), a reviewed commit counts as the baseline only if it descends from the current merge base with the default branch.

Suppose the agent gets a clean review of commit R, then merges a newer `origin/master` (call it U). The merge base becomes U. R is not a descendant of U, so R is skipped and the baseline falls back to U. The reviewer then reads all of the branch's work again, not just the merge. A rebase has the same effect.

## Proposal 1: build the baseline from the merge (recommended first)

For the latest reviewed commit R and the upstream tip U, compute `git merge-tree --write-tree R U` and use the result as the baseline:

- **Clean merge:** the computed tree equals the pushed tree, so the diff is empty and no reviewer is needed. For turn review, an empty diff already skips the reviewer (`mj-controller/src/review_host/reviewer.rs:223-238`). I did not confirm whether push review records the reviewed tree on that path. It may need a small change.
- **Merge with conflicts:** `merge-tree` writes a tree that contains the conflict markers. The diff from that tree to the pushed tree is only the conflict resolution, which is what `git show --remerge-diff` shows. The reviewer reads a few hunks instead of the whole branch. I would keep these reviews. Dropping one side of a conflict is a common bug, and "straightforward" would otherwise be the agent's own judgment.
- **Git version:** the code base already requires Git 2.38 for `merge-tree --write-tree` (`mj-checkpoint/src/archive/git.rs:1072`).
- **Limit:** a merge with no text conflicts can still break the build, for example when upstream renames a function the branch calls. A reviewer reading the full diff would rarely catch this either. Tests are the right check for it.

## Proposal 2: skip documentation by path (optional, off by default)

This would be a setting you control, for example `[review] skip_paths = ["docs/src/content/docs/**"]`. If the diff (using Proposal 1's baseline) touches only matching paths, Mjolnir records the tree as clean and adds a transcript notice that names the rule. Some cautions for this repo:

- `*.md` is too broad a pattern:
  - `mj-core/assets/skills/mj/references/*.md` ships in the binary as agent instructions.
  - `.agents/plans/` and `CLAUDE.md` steer agents.
- The doc pages describe how the code behaves, and the reviewer checks those descriptions for accuracy. Skipping documentation saves cost but drops that accuracy check. A middle option is one reviewer instead of two for changes that touch only documentation.

## What I would not do

I would not let the agent waive review itself, for example with `override_review` before any verdict exists, or with a new "trivial change" tool. Even with an audit record, the agent being reviewed would choose when to skip, and agents tend to call most of their own changes trivial. `git push --no-verify` already exists as an unchecked way around the gate.

**Recommendation:** Do Proposal 1 first. It removes the most expensive case without any policy judgment. Every pushed tree would still be reviewed work, plus published upstream work, plus reviewed conflict resolutions. Add Proposal 2 only if you want it, with narrow paths.

**Unknown:** how often merge re-reviews happen in practice. A child could count them from the session history if that would help you decide.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The gate works on Git trees, not commits (`refs/mj/reviewed/<tree>`). This is why a clean merge result can be checked mechanically: if two inputs produce exactly the same tree, nothing new was written.
- `merge-tree --write-tree` works on objects only. It never touches the index or the working tree, so it fits the rule that capture code only reads (`capture.rs:23`).
- Both proposals change only the baseline. The existing path that handles an empty diff, and the existing way of recording a reviewed tree, would do the rest, so there is no second approval route.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Supported LTS releases that ship a Git older than 2.38:**

| Distro | Git it ships | Support status |
|---|---|---|
| **Ubuntu 22.04 LTS** | 2.34.1 | Standard support until April 2027. This is the main one. |
| Ubuntu 20.04 LTS | 2.25.1 | Standard support ended May 2025; paid ESM only. |
| Debian 11 | 2.30.2 | LTS ended August 2026. |

Supported LTS releases that already have 2.38 or newer:

- Ubuntu 24.04: 2.43
- Debian 12: 2.39.5
- Debian 13: newer than that
- RHEL 8.10 (and Alma, Rocky and Oracle 8): [2.43.x in AppStream](https://repo2.msvsphere-os.ru/msvsphere/8/distroscope/en/packages/g/gi/git-0:2.43.7-1.el8_10.x86_64.html). This comes from mirror listings, not Red Hat's own pages.

- macOS with current Xcode tools: 2.39 or newer

I am fairly confident of the Ubuntu and Debian versions from memory, but I did not look them up. I did not check RHEL 9 or SLES. They are likely newer than 2.38, but that is unconfirmed.

**What this means for you:** the Git 2.25.1 case in this repo is one of your own SSH machines. `.agents/plans/git-startup-recovery.md:20` records it for the `bifrost-fuzz` checkout, which is likely Ubuntu 20.04. Any Ubuntu 22.04 host or container would also lack 2.38.

**There are two ways to have a single implementation:**

1. **`git merge-tree --write-tree` only. If Git is too old, the review fails with a clear message, for example "this review needs Git 2.38 or later".** The failure happens only when a merge follows a review. Merges detect renames, and the code stays the simplest. The cost: on Ubuntu 20.04 or 22.04, an agent that merges after a review cannot get that review and cannot push until Git is upgraded.
2. **`merge_trees` only, the helper that turn review already uses.** It works on every Git and keeps one merge mechanism for both review modes. The cost: it does not detect renames. A merge where upstream renamed a file that the branch changed gets a small review instead of none. That review is still safe.

**Recommendation:** option 1, if you are willing to upgrade Git on the 20.04 machine, or accept that agents on Ubuntu 22.04 hosts or containers cannot push after a merge that follows a review until Git is upgraded. It gives exact results, and the failure is visible rather than silent. If you need push review to keep working on those machines, option 2 is the correct single implementation. Tell me which one and I'll make the change.

fn merged_review_tree(
    runner: &dyn GitCommandRunner,
    root: &Path,
    reviewed: &str,

    let output = run(
        runner,
        root,

            "merge-tree",
            "--write-tree",
            "--allow-unrelated-histories",
            "--no-messages",
            "--name-only",

            reviewed,
            merge_base_commit,

            output.status,

/// The mode and object of each of `paths` that `tree_ish` holds.
fn tree_entries(
    runner: &dyn GitCommandRunner,
    root: &Path,
    tree_ish: &str,
    paths: &BTreeSet<PathBuf>,
) -> Result<BTreeMap<PathBuf, Vec<u8>>> {

        .collect())

It also tells it that the relay protocol moved from 49 to 50, so running sessions need the daemon handoff and a worker upgrade after the install.

**What 2.66.0 will change in before-push review:**

- **Merges:** after an agent merges newer default-branch commits into reviewed work, the review starts from `git merge-tree` of the two. A clean merge needs no reviewer. A merge with conflicts gets a review of only the conflict resolutions and any later edits. Conflicts that Git cannot mark, such as binary, modify/delete or submodule conflicts, are shown in full when the agent kept the version Git chose.
- **Default branch:** Mjolnir now finds it through `origin/main` and `origin/master` when `origin/HEAD` is missing. Your mj clones need this, because they have no `origin/HEAD`.
- **Unchanged trees:** a push whose tree is identical to its base is recorded clean without a reviewer.
- **Git version:** Git 2.39.5 is now the minimum. `mj doctor` reports older Git as fixable. With older Git, a merged push goes through without review and a warning appears in the conversation.
- **Submodules:** review diffs now always show submodule changes, whatever `diff.ignoreSubmodules` says. This applies to turn review too.

The release session will report back on its own. I am not waiting on anything else.

## Short answers

1. **Yes, but not many.** About 79% of the 27,793 slow calls are builds or tests. Most of the rest are waits on background builds and tests. The real exceptions are benchmark and measurement runs, conversation compaction, mj-agents MCP calls and waits for a human.
2. **Yes, agents mostly scope tests narrowly.** No one is "testing the world". Where scope is wrong, it is more often too narrow than too broad.

**Scope:** sessions in the `bifrost`, `bifrost2` and `bifrost-dev` bundles (all BrokkAi/bifrost-dev), 2026-10-28 to 2026-11-04. That gives 27,793 tool calls over 60 s across 2,581 sessions.

**What "duration" means here:** for Codex, the recorded time is how long the command ran, not how long the agent waited. Codex gets control back after about 7 s (median) and keeps working while the build runs. I confirmed this from transcripts. So "took over 1 minute" mostly means "a process ran over 1 minute in the background".

## 1. Slow calls that are not builds or tests

## Short answer

**Evaluate build cost, yes. But don't start from the assumption that splitting packages is the fix.** The data shows that test runs are slow because of building. It does not yet show that package structure is the reason the builds are slow.

## What the data shows (confirmed)

- **Running the tests is about 3% of a test call.** 2,728 runs printed the nextest summary line. In those runs, executing the tests took a median of 8.7 s out of a 258 s call. The median run executed **2 tests**. So agents already choose very few tests, and the rest of the time is spent building.
- **Where cargo printed its build time, the build was almost the whole call.** Examples: `Finished … in 10m 42s` in a 646 s call, and `16m 47s` in a 1,011 s call.
- **34% of test calls (618 of 1,516 hours) use the optimized `measure` profile.** In `Cargo.toml`, `[profile.measure]` inherits from `release` with LTO turned off. These calls have a median of 358 s, against 244 s for test-profile calls. An optimized build compiles much more slowly, even when the run only checks correctness.
- **Waiting for cargo's file lock is rare.** It appears in 53 of 12,233 runs, so agents fighting over one target directory is not the main cause.

## Why splitting may not help

Splitting a package shortens builds in only two situations:
1. An edit to a widely used crate forces many other crates to recompile.
2. Most of the time goes to linking the large root-package test binaries (`suite_bench_policy`, `suite_semantic` and others), which pull in the whole workspace.

Three other causes are also possible, and splitting does nothing for them:
- **Cold or missed caches.** A 10–20 minute build looks like most dependencies were compiled from scratch, not like an incremental rebuild. This could come from new lanes or worktrees, mbx misses, or many different `--features` combinations.
- **The optimized profile** used for runs that only check correctness.
- **Host contention.** Many agents build at once with `nice -n 10`, which makes builds slower in wall-clock time without changing how much work they do.

The repo already has 31 crates and a crate-splitting tool (`scripts/crate-split/`), so the easy splits have probably already been made.

## Recommendation

Before any restructuring, measure about 20 typical slow runs and break each one down:
- Which crates were recompiled, and was each recompile caused by the agent's edit, a cold cache, the profile, or a feature change?
- How long did linking take?

Rerunning those runs with `cargo build --timings` gives this breakdown. Comparing mbx hit and miss rates also helps.

- If most of the time goes to recompiling crates that depend on a frequently edited crate, or to linking the root test binaries, then splitting (or giving the integration suites fewer dependencies) is worth designing.
- If most of the time goes to cold caches, the `measure` profile or feature changes, the fix is in workflow or caching, and it is much cheaper.

I can delegate that measurement if you want it. It needs builds on the host, so I'd ask first which machine to use and whether it may compete with running agents.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- A median of "2 tests run" in a 4-minute call settles question 2 more firmly than the scope census did. Agents are already selecting tests very precisely. Their remaining cost is build cost, which choosing fewer tests cannot reduce.
- `profile.measure` was added on 2026-10-26 (see the comment above it in `Cargo.toml`) to make performance measurements comparable. Agents seem to use it for correctness tests as well, possibly to reuse one build for both. If that is a workflow habit, not a requirement, it would cost much less to fix than a package split.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## 1. Does mbx have these stats already?

**Yes. Recommending `cargo build --timings` was a mistake.** mbx 1.28.0 already has the breakdown I proposed:

- **`mbx analyze`** ranks the uncached compile time of a workspace's most recent build by cause, and says what would remove each cause. It charges a crate rebuilt only because a dependency changed to the change that started it. It also prints the critical path and the time when only one unit was compiling. It runs nothing; it reads the build mbx already recorded.
- **`mbx explain --last`** explains every cache miss in the last build by comparing it with an earlier recording of the same compilation unit.
- **`mbx stats`** shows lifetime cache savings and how much is shared across workspaces.

This answers the question directly: is build time driven by recompiling crates downstream of edits (where splitting helps), or by cache misses, profile or feature changes (where it doesn't)? One limit: `analyze` reads only the newest build *per workspace*. Each agent lane or worktree is its own workspace, though, so running it across the existing lanes should give a usable sample without building anything.

## 2. Is `measure` like O1?

**No. `measure` uses release optimization (opt-level 3) with LTO turned off.** This is confirmed on bifrost `origin/master`:

- `Cargo.toml:343` defines `[profile.measure]` as `inherits = "release"`, `lto = false`, `strip = "debuginfo"`.
- `[profile.release]` (line 327) sets only `lto = "thin"` and `strip`. Neither profile sets `opt-level` anywhere, so both use Cargo's release default of 3.
- `.cargo/config.toml` has no profile overrides or `RUSTFLAGS`.
- The agents' commands override only LTO and debug info (`CARGO_PROFILE_MEASURE_LTO=false` 420 times, `CARGO_PROFILE_*_DEBUG=0` 120 times). None of them lowers `opt-level`.

The comment above the profile states the intent: *"the same optimization without LTO, so a build costs about half the CPU (#6738)."* So the design was always "release minus LTO", not a lower optimization level. If you remember deciding on O1, that decision did not reach `master`.

That matters for the cost question. About a third of test calls (618 hours) build at opt-level 3 only to run a median of 2 tests. An O1 profile, or the test profile for runs that only check correctness, could shorten those builds a lot. That is likely but not measured. It would also be much cheaper than splitting packages.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- In Cargo, `inherits = "release"` copies every setting that is not overridden, including the default `opt-level = 3`. A profile named "measure" therefore builds at full optimization unless it says otherwise. The comment also confirms that full optimization was intended, so that measurements match release builds.
- `mbx analyze` charges a crate that rebuilt only because a dependency changed to the change that started it. That is exactly the measure needed for a split decision: it shows which edited crates make the most other crates rebuild.

## Result

**mbx could not answer the question, because of two problems in mbx itself.** The evidence available still does not justify splitting crates.

### What blocked the analysis (confirmed)

1. **`mbx analyze` and `mbx explain --last` fail inside nested lanes.** The child ran them in `~/Projects/bifrost/.mj/clones/07d292ca…/.mj/lanes/9947`, which has its own build record. Both commands failed with: `no recorded build was found for /home/jonathan/Projects/bifrost`. mbx looked up the outermost workspace above the lane, not the lane itself. The same thing happened for `bifrost3` lanes and for lanes under `/tmp`, which resolved to `/tmp`. Agents in bifrost build almost entirely in nested lanes like these, so these commands cannot be used on their builds. This looks like a bug in how mbx finds the workspace, but I have not checked the mbx source.
2. **The detailed build records do not cover the week we studied.** mbx kept one summary record per workspace for each day from Oct 28 to Nov 4 (772 workspaces). The detailed records that `analyze` and `explain` need existed only for Nov 5. The week of slow calls we studied cannot be analysed after the fact.

### What the Nov 5 data shows

This sample covers 337 builds in 21 workspaces. The hours are summed compiler time across builds that ran at the same time, not wall-clock time.

| Outcome | Compiler hours |
|---|---:|
| Never checked the cache ("unconsulted", often incremental) | 6.4 |
| Cache miss | 4.8 |
| Hit (wrapper overhead only) | ~0 |

- 86% of the builds that did check the cache found a hit. The larger cost is the **55% of uncached time that never checked the cache at all**.
- Five library crates (store, analysis, policy, semantic, flow) take 35% of uncached time. `store` alone compiled 137 times that day, up to 147 s each.
- The root `suite_*` integration test binaries take only 8%. Linking them is not the main cost.
- Only 5 of the 337 builds used `measure`. This day therefore cannot test the profile theory, which rests on the earlier week where 34% of test calls used `measure`.

### Recommendation

1. **Fix the mbx problems first.** Make `analyze` and `explain` find the nested lane's own workspace, and keep detailed records long enough to cover a week. Without that, no one can tell whether the cost comes from many crates rebuilding after edits to shared crates, which splitting would help, or from cache misses and incremental rebuilds, which it would not.
2. **Find out why so much work never checks the cache.** Of the possible causes, this is the most promising one to look at in mbx.
3. **Run a matched comparison of the `measure` and `test` profiles** on correctness-only test runs. It is still the cheapest experiment.

Then decide about splitting crates, using a week of `analyze` output.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Cargo starts at the current folder and stops at the first `Cargo.toml` that declares a workspace. In this case that is the lane itself. mbx's lookup went all the way up to `~/Projects/bifrost`. Any tool that runs in mj clones or lanes inside a repo has to stop at the nearest workspace, or it will mix up nested checkouts. That applies to mbx too.
- "Unconsulted" usually means incremental compilation of crates in the workspace, which mbx does not look up in its cache. With 21 lanes rebuilding the same `store` crate 137 times in one day, sharing those rebuilds between lanes may matter more than the layout of the crates.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## 1. What are "nested lanes", and why doesn't mbx expect them?

A **nested lane** is a checkout inside another checkout. In bifrost, mj puts each session's clone inside the main repo, at `~/Projects/bifrost/.mj/clones/<id>/`. Agents then create their own git worktrees inside that clone, at `.mj/lanes/<name>`. For example, `git worktree add --detach .mj/lanes/8640-v11b <sha>`. So a lane sits three Cargo workspaces deep: the lane, then the clone, then `~/Projects/bifrost`.

**Why mbx gets this wrong (confirmed in the source):** `workspace_root` in `crates/mbx/src/util.rs:80` walks up through every parent folder and keeps the **outermost** folder that has a `Cargo.lock`. Only `.delta/worktrees` roots stop it. The comment explains the choice: *"Ordinary VCS markers are not boundaries here: a Cargo workspace may legitimately contain a nested repository."* So mbx assumes that a nested repo is part of the outer workspace. mj's `.mj/clones` and `.mj/lanes` folders break that assumption. Cargo itself stops at the nearest folder whose `Cargo.toml` declares a workspace, which is the lane. The code is the same on the newest release branch (`7fda75b`).
